Write each set difference as an intersection with a complement of a set. Applying De Morgan's laws and then the distributive property gives
A∖(B∪C)A∖(B∩C)​=A∩B∪C=A∩(B∩C)=(A∖B)∩(A∖C),=A∩B∩C=A∩(B∪C)=(A∖B)∪(A∖C).​
(1)
The complements turn the inner union into an intersection and vice versa. Thus
A∖(B∪C)=(A∖B)∩(A∖C),A∖(B∩C)=(A∖B)∪(A∖C).​
(2)

(A∩B)∖C(A∪B)∖C​=(A∩B)∩C=(A∩C)∩(B∩C),=(A∪B)∩C=(A∩C)∪(B∩C).​
(3)
In the first line the repeated factor C changes nothing. Rewriting in terms of set differences yields
(A∩B)∖C=(A∖C)∩(B∖C),(A∪B)∖C=(A∖C)∪(B∖C).​
(4)

b OurBigBook.com
Use De Morgan's laws to remove the complement of a set, then distribute the two unions:
(A∪B)∖(A∩B)​=(A∪B)∩(A∪B)=(A∩A)∪(A∩B)∪(B∩A)∪(B∩B)=(A∩B)∪(B∩A).​
(5)
The first and last intersections in the middle line are the empty set. The remaining union is precisely the collection of elements belonging to exactly one of the original sets. Therefore both expressions define the same symmetric difference:
(A∪B)∖(A∩B)=(A∖B)∪(B∖A)=A⊕B.​
(6)

An algebraic way to prove the set identity is to show that D=A∪B is a complement of a set for A∩B. By the distributive property,
(A∩B)∩D=(A∩B∩A)∪(A∩B∩B)=∅,
(7)
and
(A∩B)∪D=(A∪D)∩(B∪D)=U∩U=U.
(8)
A complement of a set is unique: if D,E both complement S, then D=D∩(S∪E)=D∩E, and similarly E=D∩E. Consequently
A∩B=A∪B.​

The function is surjective, also called onto, when every element of its codomain has at least one preimage:
f(A)=B⟺∀b∈B ∃a∈A: f(a)=b.​
(14)
The condition concerns the specified codomain, not just the formula defining the function.

The function is injective, also called one-to-one, when equal outputs force equal inputs:
∀a,a′∈A,f(a)=f(a′)⟹a=a′.​
(15)
Equivalently, different elements of the domain of a function always have different images.

A bijection is a function that is both injective and surjective. Each element of the codomain then has exactly one preimage:
∀b∈B ∃!a∈A: f(a)=b.​
(16)
This unique-preimage property allows the inverse function f−1:B→A to be defined on all of B.

If n is positive and odd, n2 is odd. The function x↦xn2 is a strictly increasing function on the real numbers, so it is injective. Every real y has the real odd root sgn(y)∣y∣1/n2, so the function is also surjective.
If n is positive and even, the exponent is positive and even. Then f(1)=f(−1), while f(x)≥0 for all real x. These facts disprove injectivity and surjectivity, respectively. Therefore
f is onto iff n is odd;f is one-to-one iff n is odd.​
(17)
If the convention 0∈N is used, n=0 gives exponent zero. Interpreting x0 as the constant polynomial 1 makes the function neither injective nor surjective. If 00 is left undefined, that case does not define the stated function on all the real numbers. Neither convention adds a qualifying value of n.

((f∘g)∘(f−1∘g−1))(x)=2(x/2−1)+1=x−1.

First consider powers of four, with a fixed finite base value. For a mathematical induction hypothesis xn/4​≤C(n/4)2, the recurrence relation gives
xn​≤4C(n/4)2+n2=(C/4+1)n2≤Cn2
(39)
provided C≥4/3 and C also covers the base value.
The allowed integer rounding needs a little more care. Suppose the recurrence relation is applied above fixed base cases, as usual; applying x1​=4x1​+1 with a ceiling would not define a positive sequence. For either rounding write m=⌈n/4⌉ or m=⌊n/4⌋. For n≥6,
m≤4n+3​,n24m2​≤41​(1+n3​)2≤169​,m<n.
(40)
Choose C≥16/7 large enough to bound all finitely many positive-index base values below 6. By strong induction,
xn​=4xm​+n2≤4Cm2+n2≤(9C/16+1)n2≤Cn2.
(41)
This argument starts at n=6, so the floor convention's index zero, if used in an earlier base calculation, is absorbed into those fixed initial values. Thus, for either convention with a well-defined finite base,
xn​=O(n2).​
(42)

In modular arithmetic, calculations may be performed after replacing each input by its remainder. For a positive modulus m, write [a]m​ for the remainder in {0,…,m−1}. Then
[a+b]m​[ab]m​[ak]m​​=[[a]m​+[b]m​]m​,=[[a]m​[b]m​]m​,=[[a]mk​]m​(k≥0).​​
(43)
Equivalently, if a≡a′(modm) and b≡b′(modm), addition and multiplication give a+b≡a′+b′ and ab≡a′b′, and a fixed nonnegative integer exponent gives ak≡(a′)k. One cannot in general reduce the exponent modulo m by this rule.

Mathematical induction has two obligations. Establish the base case S(0) if the natural numbers start at zero, or S(1) if they start at one. Then prove the induction step: for an arbitrary natural k in the relevant range, assume S(k) and deduce S(k+1).
The base case starts the chain, and the step propagates truth to every subsequent natural number:
S(n0​) ∧ (∀k≥n0​, S(k)⇒S(k+1)) ⟹ ∀n≥n0​, S(n).​
(48)

The base case is F5​=5, so 5∣F5​. To relate successive blocks of five, use the Fibonacci addition formula:
Fk+5​=F5​Fk+1​+F4​Fk​=5Fk+1​+3Fk​.
(49)
This identity can also be obtained simply by applying the Fibonacci recurrence five times. If the mathematical induction hypothesis is 5∣F5n​, then
F5(n+1)​=5F5n+1​+3F5n​
(50)
is a sum of two multiples of five. Hence
F5​∣F5n​for every integer n>0.​
(51)
The generalisation is Fibonacci multiple-index divisibility:
Fm​∣Fmn​(m,n≥1).​
(52)
Indeed, Fmn+m​=Fm​Fmn+1​+Fm−1​Fmn​, so precisely the same mathematical induction works with 5 replaced by m.

d OurBigBook.com
A binary relation R on A is a subset of A×A. Its properties are quantified over elements of A:
  • A reflexive relation satisfies ∀a∈A, aRa.
  • A symmetric relation satisfies ∀a,b∈A, aRb⇒bRa.
  • An antisymmetric relation satisfies ∀a,b∈A, (aRb∧bRa)⇒a=b.
  • A transitive relation satisfies ∀a,b,c∈A, (aRb∧bRc)⇒aRc.
  • An irreflexive relation satisfies ∀a∈A, ¬(aRa).
  • A serial relation satisfies ∀a∈A ∃b∈A, aRb.
Thus an equivalence relation is a binary relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The equivalence class of a is the set of all elements related to it:
R is an equivalence relation⟺R is reflexive, symmetric and transitive;[a]R​={b∈A:aRb}.​
(55)
Antisymmetry permits diagonal pairs and does not mean that a binary relation fails to be a symmetric relation.

This is equality of remainders in modular arithmetic. It is reflexive because 3∣(n−n)=0, symmetric because 3∣(n−m) implies 3∣(m−n), and transitive because 3∣(n−m) and 3∣(k−n) imply 3∣(k−m) by addition. Thus
m∼n⟺m≡n(mod3) is an equivalence relation.​
(57)
Its three equivalence classes are
Cr​={n∈N:n≡r(mod3)},r=0,1,2.​
(58)
If zero is included in N, it belongs to C0​; otherwise that class starts at three.

In a symmetric relation, each of the n diagonal pairs (a,a) can be chosen independently. For each of the (2n​) unordered pairs of distinct elements, either both ordered pairs (a,b),(b,a) occur or neither occurs. Every such choice is free and produces a distinct symmetric relation. Hence
2n2(2n​)=2n(n+1)/2.​
(59)
For the empty set this correctly gives one binary relation, the empty one.

Let H mean the added ball was red, and D mean the first draw was red. Their relevant probabilities are P(H)=P(Hc)=1/2, P(D∣H)=1, and P(D∣Hc)=1/2. The law of total probability gives P(D)=3/4.
Given the observed red draw, the remaining ball is red precisely when H occurred. Bayes' theorem therefore gives
P(remaining ball red∣D)=P(H∣D)=3/41⋅(1/2)​=32​.​
(96)
The observation increases the weight of the two-red-ball box, because that box is more likely to yield a red first draw.

Let B count the red balls among the n added balls. By independence of random variables, B has a binomial distribution with parameters n,1/2. The total red count is R=1+B, and the box has n+1 balls. Conditional on R=r, sampling without replacement gives
P(D1​∣R=r)=n+1r​,P(D1​∩D2​∣R=r)=n(n+1)r(r−1)​,
(97)
where D1​,D2​ denote red first and second draws. Averaging these conditional probabilities and taking their ratio gives
P(D2​∣D1​)=nE[R]E[R(R−1)]​.
(98)
The binomial distribution moments give E[B]=n/2 and E[B2]=n/4+n2/4. Consequently
E[R]=2n+2​,E[R(R−1)]=E[B2+B]=4n(n+3)​.
(99)
Therefore the red-ball prediction with one certain red ball is
P(D2​∣D1​)=2(n+2)n+3​,n≥1.​
(100)
It reduces to 2/3 at n=1 and approaches 1/2 as the number of randomly coloured extra balls grows. Taking an unweighted average of the remaining red fractions would miss the change in weights caused by taking a conditional probability given the first red draw.

This numbered item specifies the model used below. A convenient sample space is the collection of 36 ordered pairs (s1​,s2​)∈{1,…,6}2, each with probability 1/36. The corresponding random variables are determined by the sum and difference. Inverting the two equations gives
S1​=2X+Y​,S2​=2X−Y​.​

Thus a candidate pair (X,Y)=(i,j) is possible exactly when (i+j)/2 and (i−j)/2 are both integers between 1 and 6. In particular, i and j must have the same parity. This inverse description will determine the joint probability mass function.

Put ai​=6−∣i−7∣ and bj​=6−∣j∣. If the two events were independent, a feasible pair would require
361​=36ai​​36bj​​,so ai​bj​=36.

Since 1≤ai​,bj​≤6, equality forces ai​=bj​=6, hence (i,j)=(7,0). But that pair is infeasible. An infeasible pair cannot give independence either, since its joint probability is zero while the product of its positive marginal probabilities is positive. Thus
There are no independent pairs of these events within the two marginal supports.​

If all real values of i,j are allowed literally, an impossible event is independent of every event. The complete answer without a support restriction is therefore
{X=i} and {Y=j} are independent iff i∈/{2,…,12} or j∈/{−5,…,5}.​
